name: Harpaz benchmark
description: Media coverage, regulatory communications, and litigation stimulate spontaneous adverse event reporting (notoriety bias). This study asks whether adjusting for measured public attention improves drug safety signal detection. It does four things: 1. Point-in-time database. We reconstructed the U.S. Food and Drug Administration adverse event reporting systems (FAERS 2012Q4–2026Q2 and legacy AERS 2004Q1–2012Q3; 24.8 million report records, 20.6 million unique cases). Each case version is valid from its receipt until it is superseded or deleted, so analyses can use only the information available at a given date. 2. Descriptive analyses. We measured how reporting disproportionality changed around media, regulatory, and litigation events for 22 drug–event pairs, using Google Trends, Wikipedia pageviews, PubMed counts, and dated FDA, EMA, WHO, and court events. 3. Models and simulation. We fitted attention-driven excitation models (negative binomial, with and without self-excitation) and evaluated them in a simulation study of 7 scenarios with 500 replicates each. 4. Protocol-based benchmark. We compared five signal-detection methods on the 137-pair Harpaz time-indexed reference standard, using only information available before each labeling change. The evaluation protocol was dated and frozen before any result was computed, but it was not publicly preregistered. Main result: adjusting for drug-level attention reduced signal detection.
